newsitem.title: USA: Fed likely to follow up rate rise with more.
newsitem.headline: Fed likely to follow up rate rise with more.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The U.S. Federal Reserve is likely to follow up this week's rise in interest rates with at least one more increase in the months ahead as it struggles to stay ahead of inflation, analysts said.

"Usually they raise rates a number of times ... Normally when they start raising rates they end up raising them by at least 1 percent," said William Ford, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

The central bank on Tuesday increased interest rates for the first time in more than two years, bumping up its target for the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans to 5.5 percent from 5.25 percent.
It left the less important discount rate it charges the banks for money unchanged at 5.0 percent.
Major banks quickly matched the Fed's move, boosting their prime lending rates for business customers to 8.50 percent from 8.25 percent.
The moves will mean higher borrowing costs for a variety of consumers and companies, from credit card users to the stores where they shop.
The Fed described its rate rise as a "prudent step" designed to help prolong the economic expansion by keeping inflation low through the end of next year.
"This action was taken in light of persisting strength in demand, which is progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances developing in the economy," it added.
Several economists said the Fed's statement left the door open to further rate increases, possibly as soon as the central bank's next policy-making meeting on May 20.
Much will depend on the course of the economy in the coming months, they said. If the economy stays strong, further rate increases are likely. If it slows, Tuesday's rate increase could be the last.

In the first data following the Fed's action, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday that orders for costly manufactured goods climbed 1.5 percent in February to a seasonally adjusted record $178.3 billion.

"The bottom line is if the economy's growth is sustained -- and I think it will be at least until May -- they will move again," said Jerry Zukowski, an economist at Wall Street broker PaineWebber Inc.

After expanding at a brisk annualized rate of 3.9 percent in the fourth quarter of last year, the economy appears to have slowed slightly in the first three months of this year to a growth rate closer to 3 percent, analysts said.
Much of the slowdown has occurred in the so-called external sector, as U.S. exports have sagged and imports have soared, in part because the strong dollar has made foreign goods cheaper.

Domestic U.S. demand has stayed strong, although special factors may have played a role there. This winter was much warmer than last, spurring construction, and consumer spending has been boosted by larger-than-normal tax refunds.
Greenspan told lawmakers last week that the economy retains a "great deal of vigor" and termed the prospects of a continuation of the six-year-old expansion "quite favourable."
But he also made clear that that depended critically on the Fed staying ahead of inflation and keeping it from rising.
U.S. lawmakers attacked the Fed for increasing interest rates at a time when inflation was low and said further increases could hamper efforts to balance the federal budget.

"A rate increase will likely slow economic expansion, thus reducing the amount of revenues coming into the Federal treasury," said Sen. Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat. "This Fed muzzle on the economy will only make an already strained budget process even more difficult," he added.
U.S. companies also criticised the Fed's move.

"It is a regrettable and serious mistake," the National Association of Manufacturers said in a statement. "It will impede economic growth and make life tougher on consumers and job-creating businesses."
Tuesday's rate increase marked a reversal of Fed policy. Its last rate change came on Jan. 31, 1996, when it trimmed rates by a quarter percentage point.
